summary:
This bill is called the "Stop Disaster Price Gouging Act." It tries to stop stores and businesses from charging way too much for things after a big disaster or emergency.

Here is how it works. The President can declare a "major disaster or emergency" when something bad happens, like a big storm or flood. After that, businesses in that area must follow rules.

For important things people need — like food, water, medicine, gas, lumber, hotels, and rent — a business cannot raise the price more than 10 percent for 30 days. For fixing and rebuilding things, they cannot raise prices more than 10 percent for 180 days. Businesses also cannot charge a price that is more than 50 percent above what the item costs them.

There are some exceptions. If a business had to pay more to get the goods, or if new taxes on trade (called tariffs) raised the cost, higher prices may be allowed.

The Federal Trade Commission, a government group that watches over fair business, would enforce these rules. States and hurt people can also go to court. Businesses that break the rules can be fined up to $25,000. This amount can grow over time to keep up with rising prices.

The money collected from fines would go into a fund to help communities hit by disasters. People have up to 2 years to bring a case to court.
